definition.text: Mangrove forests are a form of natural capital that yields many goods and services to coasts, local communities and society at large.

facts.text: Some mangrove outputs, such as timber, are traded in ordinary markets, where their value shows up as a price.
Mangroves give nursery habitat to many species, including commercial fish and crustaceans, helping keep local fish and shellfish numbers up.
An estimated 75 percent of the prawns and fish caught commercially in Queensland, Australia, depend on mangroves for part of their life cycle.
Mangroves help keep water clean by cycling nutrients, and they slow water so sediment settles out.
Mangrove forests take carbon from the air and store it in their biomass and waterlogged soils, adding to coastal blue carbon stocks.
At least 35 percent of the world's mangroves were destroyed in a single decade, faster than tropical rainforests disappeared.
Economic arguments weigh most in mangrove conservation, yet the true economic value of mangroves is hard to measure and key ecological functions are undervalued.

title: Mangrove water filtration
article: Ecological values of mangroves#Improving coastal water quality

definition.text: Mangroves keep coastal water clean by trapping, removing and recycling nutrients, pollutants and particles from land before they reach reefs and seagrass.

facts.text: Mangrove roots slow the water so sediment settles, and toxins and nutrients bound to the sediment are removed with it.
Because building a wastewater treatment plant is costly, mangroves are often chosen to receive effluent, and purpose-built mangrove wetlands now treat sewage and aquaculture waste.
Runoff is filtered first by coastal forests, then mangroves, then seagrass beds before reaching coral reefs, which need these buffers to avoid algal overgrowth.

definition.text: A nutrient cycle is the movement of living and non-living matter back into the making of new living matter: nature's recycling system.

facts.text: Energy flows one way through an ecosystem and is not reused, while mineral nutrients move in cycles.
The cycles include the carbon, sulfur, nitrogen, water, phosphorus and oxygen cycles, among others.
Recycling in nature is controlled largely by decomposition, and food webs full of different species do the work.
Natural recycling is one of the ecosystem services that sustain human well-being.
Some ecosystems run a nutrient debt and act as sinks while others have a surplus and act as sources, depending on climate, landform and geology.
Most textbooks treat 'nutrient cycle' and 'biogeochemical cycle' as the same, though 'nutrient cycle' usually means cycling within one ecosystem.
In 1749 Carl Linnaeus described nature's recycling in his book Oeconomia Naturae, the 'economy of nature'.

title: Complete recycling debate

definition.text: A dispute over whether matter can be recycled completely, with 100% of waste rebuilt into new material without end.

facts.text: Howard T. Odum held that living systems can gather chemical elements without limit as long as energy, such as sunlight, is available.
In 1979 Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen proposed a 'fourth law' of entropy saying complete recycling is impossible.
The fourth law has been rejected in light of observed ecological recycling, though some authors say complete recycling is impossible for technological waste.

contested_note: Georgescu-Roegen said complete recycling is impossible; others reject this for ecosystems but some accept it for technological waste.

definition.text: Recycling in human industry differs from recycling in ecosystems in scale, complexity and organization.

facts.text: Industrial recycling relies on people and technology rather than food webs to turn waste back into marketable goods.
Only 7% of all plastic waste is recycled by industry; the other 93% is presumably absorbed by natural recycling systems.
Many human 'technoecosystems' compete with or feed off natural ecosystems.

definition.text: Biological pest control is the use of living organisms to control pests, whether animals, weeds or disease-causing organisms.

facts.text: It works through predation, parasitism and plant-eating, usually with people actively managing it, and can be part of integrated pest management.
The first known record comes from China around 304 AD, where citrus growers bought nests of predatory ants to protect their fruit.
Modern biological control began in the US in the 1870s, when state entomologists started handing out parasitoids to fight crop pests.
Agents include predators such as lady beetles, parasitoid wasps and flies, and disease organisms such as bacteria, fungi and viruses.
Bacillus thuringiensis, a soil bacterium, is the most widely used bacterial control agent, and its genes have been put into transgenic crops.
Biological control can reduce the economic losses caused by pests, disease carriers and invasive species.
Using natural enemies instead of pesticides can also cut agricultural pollution.

definition.text: Biological control comes in three basic strategies: importation, augmentation and conservation of natural enemies.

facts.text: Importation, or classical control, brings a pest's natural enemies into a new place where they did not live before.
Augmentation releases extra natural enemies: a few at intervals to prevent outbreaks (inoculative), or many at once to knock a pest down fast (inundative).
Early importations were often unofficial, and some introduced species became serious pests themselves.
Augmentative control adds more predators, parasitoids or microbes when needed.

definition.text: Conservation biological control protects and encourages the natural enemies of pests that already live in an area.

facts.text: Nectar plants grown on rice field borders cut planthopper pests 10- to 100-fold, so farmers sprayed 70% less insecticide and gained 5% in yield.
Changing cropping systems to favour natural enemies is called habitat manipulation, for example with hedgerows, shelterbelts or beetle banks.
A meter-wide strip of tussock grass in the middle of English fields let aphid predators overwinter there and improved control.

definition.text: An introduced control agent can harm biodiversity by attacking native species as well as the pest it was meant for.

facts.text: Vertebrates tend to eat many kinds of food and seldom make good control agents; many classic failures involve them.
Cane toads released in Australia in 1935 could not reach the cane beetles, spread fast instead and harmed native frogs and predators.

definition.text: Pollination is the moving of pollen from the male part of a flower to the female part, which lets the plant make seeds.

facts.text: Pollen can be carried by animals such as bees, beetles, butterflies, birds and bats, or by wind and water.
Between 100,000 and 200,000 animal species pollinate the world's 250,000 species of flowering plant, most of them insects.
About 80% of flowering plants rely on living pollinators.
Farms closer to natural habitat get more pollinator visits and higher crop yields.
Three quarters of the plant species that feed the world need pollinators, and insect-pollinated crops are worth over 200 billion dollars.
Animal pollination keeps plants genetically varied because it allows cross-breeding rather than self-breeding.

definition.text: Beekeepers rent their honeybee colonies to farmers for a fee, turning crop pollination into a service sold in a market.

facts.text: Honeybees do most pollination of the crops people eat, giving between $235 and $577 billion of benefits to global food production.
As of 2016, pollination rentals made up 41% of an average US beekeeper's revenue, the largest share of their income.
Pollination by beekeepers' bees is a positive externality that the market has managed to pay for.
The almond industry uses up to 82% of the pollination market, and each February around 60% of US bee colonies are moved to California's Central Valley.
Mixing hives spreads disease to wild bees too, a negative externality that reduces biodiversity.
In 2016 an almond colony earned $165 in rent, about three times other crops, yet once upkeep is counted almond pollination is barely profitable.

definition.text: Biotic pollination uses living animals to carry pollen, while abiotic pollination relies on wind, water or rain.

facts.text: Some 98% of abiotic pollination is by wind.
Abiotic pollination lets a plant spend its energy on pollen rather than on flowers and nectar to attract animals.
Some plants use both kinds, such as an orchid pollinated by rain or butterflies depending on conditions.

definition.text: Many farm crops depend on pollinators, while the main staple grains such as wheat, maize and rice are pollinated by wind or by themselves.

facts.text: Among the top 15 crops in 2013, slightly over 10% of the human plant diet (211 of 1916 kcal per person per day) depended on insect pollination.
Managed US beehives fell from close to 6 million after WWII to under 2.5 million, while bee-pollinated crop area grew over 300%.
About one million hives, nearly half of US honey bees, are trucked to California almond orchards each spring.

title: Pollinator decline

definition.text: Pollinator decline is the drop in numbers of insect and other animal pollinators in many ecosystems around the world, recorded since the end of the 20th century.

facts.text: Evidence of falling wild pollinator numbers is strongest in Europe and North America, with similar findings from South America, China and Japan.
Managed honey bee colonies fell 25% in Europe (1985–2005) and 59% in North America (1947–2005), but global stocks rose thanks to China and Argentina.
While managed hives grew by 45%, demand for animal-pollinated crops tripled, showing the risk of relying on domesticated bees.
A 2021 century-long study found the number of bee species recorded in 2006–2015 was a quarter lower than before 1990.
About 87.5% of flowering plant species and 60% of crop species use animal pollinators, including most fruits.
Without animal pollination, US farm output is expected to fall by 3 to 8%.
In 2009 a study valued the 100 crops that need pollinators at €153 billion worldwide.
So far the theorised decline has not cut food production: yields of animal-pollinated and other crops have risen at the same rate.

contested_note: Sources disagree on how serious the decline is: some warn of falling food supplies, while others note crop yields have not yet suffered.

definition.text: Proposed causes of pollinator decline include pesticides, parasites and diseases, habitat destruction, climate change, market forces and competition with invasive species.

facts.text: Synthetic pesticides, above all neonicotinoids, are a primary driver, damaging the nerves and immune systems of bees and other pollinators.
Air pollution breaks down flower scents so they travel shorter distances, forcing pollinators to fly farther to find flowers.
Climate change can make bees emerge when no plants are flowering.
A 2021 global assessment said policy should focus on land-cover change, land management and pesticides.

definition.text: Losing pollinators could cut the supply of vitamins and other nutrients that come mainly from animal-pollinated crops.

facts.text: An estimated 70% of dietary vitamin A and 55% of folate worldwide come from animal-pollinated crops.
If all pollinators died off, a 2015 model found 71 million more people in low-income countries would lack vitamin A.
The same model predicted 1.42 million extra deaths a year, or 700,000 if half of pollinators were lost.

definition.text: Seed dispersal is split into autochory, where the plant moves its own seeds, and allochory, where an outside agent carries them.

facts.text: Self-dispersal uses gravity or exploding fruit, which limits how far seeds go; the dynamite tree can throw seeds up to 100 meters.
Outside agents include wind, water and animals; seeds can ride on animals' fur or pass through their guts.
Humans move seeds on clothes (up to 250 m), shoes (up to 5 km) and cars (sometimes over 100 km).

definition.text: Water purification is the removal of unwanted chemicals, germs, suspended solids and gases from water so it is fit for a given use.

facts.text: Purifying water is a regulating ecosystem service: New York City restored its polluted Catskill Watershed rather than rely only on treatment when its water fell below EPA standards.
Soil and rock layers naturally filter groundwater so well that it often needs only a disinfectant added.
In bank filtration, natural riverbank sediments give the first stage of cleaning, and slow sand filters work through biological processes rather than straining.
Engineered treatment uses physical steps such as filtration and sedimentation, chemical steps such as chlorination, and biological steps.
A diverse aquatic plant community helps purify water for human use.
A 2007 WHO report said 1.1 billion people lacked an improved drinking water supply and 1.8 million died from diarrhoeal disease each year.

title: Bioprospecting

definition.text: Bioprospecting is the search through living things for molecules and genetic information that could become valuable products such as drugs, cosmetics or farm inputs.

facts.text: Almost one third of small-molecule drugs approved by the US FDA between 1981 and 2014 were natural products or derived from them.
Many antibiotics in use today came from bioprospecting, such as streptomycin from a soil bacterium; the antimalarial artemisinin came from a plant.
Natural molecules are more structurally complex than synthetic ones, so they act on biological targets more precisely.
Researchers now look beyond plants and soil microbes to seas, caves, polar regions and extremophiles.
Over-harvesting desirable species for bioprospecting can push them toward extinction.
The UN and others promote bioprospecting as ethical development based on protecting biodiversity, but critics say conservation areas shut local people out of common lands.

contested_note: Bioprospecting is promoted as sustainable development but criticised for excluding local communities and exploiting their knowledge.

definition.text: Bioprospecting contracts set the rules for sharing benefits between researchers and the countries whose genetic resources they use.

facts.text: The Convention on Biological Diversity, in force from 1993, gave countries the right to control access to their genetic resources, creating this branch of law.
The contracts rest on prior informed consent and compensation and can bring royalties to poorer countries, yet not every knowledge holder is consulted or paid.
Biodiverse countries expect a share of the benefits rather than letting the discoverer keep them privately.

definition.text: Firewood is any wood used for fuel, usually as recognizable logs or branches rather than processed products such as pellets.

facts.text: Firewood is a renewable resource, but local demand can quickly outrun how fast trees regrow.
For most of human history firewood was the main fuel, and the right to gather it was a valued part of many medieval leases.
Along with clearing land for farming, gathering firewood is a cause of deforestation, and its smoke causes breathing problems.
Moving firewood long distances can spread tree pests, diseases and invasive species.

definition.text: Food security means having reliable access to enough affordable, healthy food.

facts.text: The 1996 World Food Summit defined it as all people at all times having physical and economic access to enough safe, nutritious food for an active, healthy life.
Close to 12% of the world's people, 928 million, were severely food insecure in 2020, 148 million more than in 2019.
Hunger is often caused not by a lack of food but by people being unable to reach the food that exists, usually because of poverty.
Intensive farming can trap land in a cycle of falling soil fertility and falling yields; deforestation and overgrazing also degrade land.
Overfishing poses serious risks to food security.
Losing crop diversity threatens food security because people rely on fewer and fewer varieties of fewer crop species.
Pollinator decline could endanger food security as well as unbalance ecosystems.

definition.text: Food security is usually broken into pillars: whether food is available, whether people can get it, how well they use it, and whether this stays stable over time.

facts.text: Availability is the supply of food through production, distribution and exchange.
Access covers whether food is affordable and how it is shared out, along with people's preferences.
Stability is the ability to get food over time; food insecurity can be passing, seasonal or chronic.
Sustainability, a further pillar, asks that food systems feed people now without undermining the bases for feeding future generations.

definition.text: Groundwater recharge is the downward movement of water from the surface into underground water stores.

facts.text: Recharge is the main way water enters an aquifer, the underground layer that holds groundwater.
It happens naturally through rain and snowmelt, and artificially when people route rainwater or reclaimed water underground.
Paving, development and logging can strip topsoil, increasing runoff and reducing recharge, while tree roots help water soak in.
Wetlands help hold up the water table; small wetlands can recharge up to 20% of their volume per season.
For groundwater use to be sustainable, the long-run rate of pumping from an aquifer should not exceed the rate it is recharged.
People move about 24,000 km3 of water a year, about double the world's yearly groundwater recharge.
Recharge rates are hard to measure because evaporation, plant transpiration and infiltration must be estimated first.
Recharge happens naturally through the water cycle and artificially when rainwater or reclaimed water is routed underground.

definition.text: Managed aquifer recharge means deliberately putting water back into aquifers, for example through altered streambeds, bank filtration, water spreading or recharge wells.

facts.text: A facility in Orange County, California cleans and injects 100 million gallons a day, or 90 billion gallons a year.
In India, where farmers' over-pumping has depleted groundwater, the government funded dug-well recharge projects in 100 districts in 2007.

definition.text: Medicinal plants are plants used to keep people healthy or treat illness, in traditional medicine since prehistoric times and in modern medicine today.

facts.text: Plants make hundreds of chemicals to defend themselves against insects, fungi and grazing animals, and these are the basis of their use as drugs.
The Food and Agriculture Organization estimated in 2002 that over 50,000 medicinal plants are used worldwide.
Around a quarter of drugs prescribed in modern medicine come from medicinal plants.
By one 2023 estimate the global market was US$68 billion a year, growing 10–20% annually; China and India lead production and export.
In much of the rural developing world, traditional herbal medicine is people's only source of health care.
Wild-harvested medicinal plants are threatened by climate change, habitat loss and over-collection to meet rising demand.
As of 2015 most plant-based products had not been tested for safety and effectiveness, and being natural does not make a product safe.

conflicts.text: Kew Gardens estimated in 2016 that 17,810 plant species have a medicinal use.
conflicts.note: A more conservative count than the FAO's 2002 figure of over 50,000.

definition.text: A microclimate is the local set of air, soil and water conditions near the ground that differs measurably from the surrounding area.

facts.text: A microclimate can be anything from a few meters to at most a few kilometers across.
Climate is described at nested scales: macroclimates span hundreds to thousands of kilometers, mesoclimates tens to hundreds, and microclimates far less.
Microclimates are shaped by terrain, soil, vegetation, water and human-made features, which change sunlight, wind, heat and moisture near the surface.
A wooded park stays different from a nearby industrial park because leaves absorb light and heat that roofs and parking lots radiate back into the air.
Farmers manage microclimates with irrigation, shading, windbreaks and vegetation to buffer crops from heat and drought, which matters more as climate extremes grow.
A clearing wider than twice the height of nearby trees loses the woodland's moderating effect on the microclimate.
Habitat fragmentation can change microclimates locally and regionally, affecting biodiversity.

definition.text: A nursery habitat is a place where young marine animals live that contributes more young to the adult population per unit area than other places they use.

facts.text: Mangroves, salt marshes and seagrass are typical nursery habitats for many marine species.
Seagrass meadows give nursery habitat to over a fifth of the world's 25 largest fisheries, including walleye pollock, the most landed species.
Losing nursery habitats can mean fewer young reaching adulthood, shrinking populations needed for both biodiversity and fishing.
Juvenile density alone is not enough evidence; the best measure is how much biomass moves from juvenile to adult populations.

definition.text: Pollination management is the farming practice of ensuring or improving a crop's pollination by managing pollinators, pollen-supplying plants and conditions.

facts.text: Besides honey bees, growers use blue orchard bees, bumblebees, hand pollination and even machines.
Too few pollinators can limit yield, called pollination limitation; it fell by 50% between 1950 and the 2010s, mainly because fields were supplied with managed pollinators.
Bigger monoculture fields make management more important; the blue orchard bee visits only the target tree and is 100 times more efficient per bee than a honeybee.
A 1950s grower of ten acres of watermelons had wild bees enough, but today's 200-acre grower must bring hives to the field.

definition.text: Soil formation, or pedogenesis, is the slow making of soil, shaped by place, environment and history.

facts.text: It starts with the weathering of fresh parent material; microbes feed on the released nutrients and leave residues that become humus.
Over time soil develops distinct layers called horizons, differing in colour, structure, texture and chemistry.
In Sicily's Mediterranean climate, weathering makes new soil at about 1/10 mm per year.
It takes decades to several thousand years for a soil to develop a profile.
Erosion from farm fields is estimated at 11 to 20 times the soil formation rate with no-till farming, and over 100 times with conventional tillage.
Soil formation is classed as a supporting ecosystem service, and food systems depend on it.
Vasily Dokuchaev, regarded as the father of soil science, showed in 1883 that soil forms over time under climate, vegetation, topography and parent material.

definition.text: Five classic factors shape every soil: climate, organisms, relief (topography), parent material and time, remembered as CLORPT.

facts.text: Climate is the dominant factor, and soils show the traits of the climate zone where they form.
Steep slopes lose soil quickly to erosion, so soils there are shallower and less developed than on nearby level ground.
Plants hold soil against erosion and build humus, while animals break down plant matter and mix the soil.
Soil is the most species-rich ecosystem on Earth, mostly microbes, many still undescribed.

definition.text: Hans Jenny's 1941 state equation describes a soil as a function of climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time, with room for more factors.

facts.text: Unlike Dokuchaev's earlier equation, it treats time as a factor, adds relief and leaves the list open.
It is mostly solved empirically, by varying one factor while holding the others constant, giving models such as climofunctions and chronofunctions.
Soil surveyors worldwide use it as a checklist of what shapes a region's soils.

definition.text: A storm surge is a coastal flood of rising seawater pushed ashore by a storm, usually a low-pressure system such as a tropical cyclone.

facts.text: It is measured as the rise in water above the normal tide, not counting waves, and is driven mainly by strong winds pushing water toward the coast.
Low air pressure raises sea level by about 10 mm for every millibar of pressure drop.
The deadliest surge on record, from the 1970 Bhola cyclone, killed up to 500,000 people around the Bay of Bengal.
Surges damage roads and buildings and also harm soil fertility, push saltwater inland and spread contaminants.
With stronger extreme weather and rising seas from climate change, surges are expected to pose greater risks to coastal people.
Tidal marshes protect coastal habitat from storm surge and flooding.

definition.text: Communities can adapt to storm surges with hard infrastructure such as flood barriers, soft infrastructure such as dunes or mangroves, better building and social measures.

facts.text: Storm-surge barriers, built after the North Sea flood of 1953, stay open for shipping but close when a surge threatens.
Major barriers include the Dutch Delta Works, the Thames Barrier and the Saint Petersburg Dam.
Warnings, education and local evacuation plans reduce the toll on people.

title: Climate regulation

definition.text: Climate regulation is the regulating ecosystem service by which nature dampens environmental change, for example by storing carbon and moderating local temperatures.

facts.text: A 1970 report that introduced the term 'environmental services' already listed climate regulation alongside pollination, fisheries and flood control.
Tropical rainforests are crucial for global climate regulation through carbon sequestration.
Mangroves regulate climate by sequestering carbon, and coastal seas also provide climate regulation.
Urban trees help regulate microclimate and take up carbon dioxide.
Climate regulation is among the services considered to have no viable substitute.
Regime shifts, such as forest turning into savanna or faster summer loss of Arctic ice, can weaken climate regulation.
Gross ecosystem product puts a money value on regulating services such as climate regulation.

notes: Phrase concept: no page of its own. Many search hits for 'climate regulation' mean government climate rules, not the ecosystem service; only service-sense sentences are cited.

title: Watershed services

definition.text: Watershed (hydrological) services are the water-related benefits a healthy catchment gives, such as less soil erosion, lower landslide risk and milder floods and droughts.

facts.text: Watershed services are one of the three main kinds of service sold in payment-for-ecosystem-services schemes, with climate mitigation and biodiversity.
Costa Rica's payment scheme explicitly recognized hydrological services among its four environmental services.
Growing markets for hydrological services may reward forests managed with low-impact logging.

notes: Phrase concept: no page of its own.
